'''Kaniadakis statistics''' (also known as '''κ-statistics''') is a generalization of [[Statistical mechanics|Boltzmann–Gibbs statistical mechanics]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2009 |title=Relativistic entropy and related Boltzmann kinetics |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1140/epja/i2009-10793-6 |journal=The European Physical Journal A |language=en |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=275–287 |article-number=275 |doi=10.1140/epja/i2009-10793-6 |arxiv=0901.1058 |bibcode=2009EPJA...40..275K |s2cid=119190011 |issn=1434-6001}}</ref> based on a [[Special relativity|relativistic]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2002 |title=Statistical mechanics in the context of special relativity |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.66.056125 |journal=Physical Review E |language=en |volume=66 |issue=5 |article-number=056125 |arxiv=cond-mat/0210467 |bibcode=2002PhRvE..66e6125K |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.66.056125 |issn=1063-651X |pmid=12513574 |s2cid=45635888}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2005 |title=Statistical mechanics in the context of special relativity. II. |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.72.036108 |journal=Physical Review E |language=en |volume=72 |issue=3 |article-number=036108 |arxiv=cond-mat/0507311 |bibcode=2005PhRvE..72c6108K |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.72.036108 |issn=1539-3755 |pmid=16241516 |s2cid=18115408}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2011 |title=Power-law tailed statistical distributions and Lorentz transformations |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0375960110015276 |journal=Physics Letters A |language=en |volume=375 |issue=3 |pages=356–359 |arxiv=1110.3944 |bibcode=2011PhLA..375..356K |doi=10.1016/j.physleta.2010.11.057 |issn=0375-9601 |s2cid=118435479}}</ref> generalization of the classical [[Boltzmann's entropy formula|Boltzmann–Gibbs–Shannon entropy]] (commonly referred to as Kaniadakis entropy or κ-entropy). Introduced by the Greek Italian [[physicist]] [[Giorgio Kaniadakis]] in 2001,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2001 |title=Non-linear kinetics underlying generalized statistics |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378437101001844 |journal=Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and Its Applications |language=en |volume=296 |issue=3 |pages=405–425 |doi=10.1016/S0378-4371(01)00184-4 |arxiv=cond-mat/0103467 |bibcode=2001PhyA..296..405K |s2cid=44275064 |issn=0378-4371}}</ref> κ-statistical mechanics preserve the main features of ordinary [[statistical mechanics]] and have attracted the interest of many researchers in recent years. The κ-distribution is currently considered one of the most viable candidates for explaining [[Complex system|complex physical]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2009 |title=Maximum entropy principle and power-law tailed distributions |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1140/epjb/e2009-00161-0 |journal=The European Physical Journal B |language=en |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=3–13 |doi=10.1140/epjb/e2009-00161-0 |arxiv=0904.4180 |bibcode=2009EPJB...70....3K |s2cid=55421804 |issn=1434-6028}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2021 |title=New power-law tailed distributions emerging in κ-statistics (a) |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/133/10002 |journal=Europhysics Letters |volume=133 |issue=1 |article-number=10002 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/133/10002 |arxiv=2203.01743 |bibcode=2021EL....13310002K |s2cid=234144356 |issn=0295-5075}}</ref> natural or artificial systems involving [[Power law|power-law]] tailed [[statistical distributions]]. Kaniadakis statistics have been adopted successfully in the description of a variety of systems in the fields of [[cosmology]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Drepanou |first1=Niki |last2=Lymperis |first2=Andreas |last3=Saridakis |first3=Emmanuel N. |last4=Yesmakhanova |first4=Kuralay |date=2022-05-16 |title=Kaniadakis holographic dark energy and cosmology |journal=The European Physical Journal C |language=en |volume=82 |issue=5 |page=449 |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-022-10415-9 |doi-access=free|arxiv=2109.09181 |bibcode=2022EPJC...82..449D |issn=1434-6052}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hernández-Almada |first1=A |last2=Leon |first2=Genly |last3=Magaña |first3=Juan |last4=García-Aspeitia |first4=Miguel A |last5=Motta |first5=V |last6=Saridakis |first6=Emmanuel N |last7=Yesmakhanova |first7=Kuralay |date=2022 |title=Kaniadakis-holographic dark energy: observational constraints and global dynamics |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |volume=511 |issue=3 |pages=4147–4158 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stac255 |doi-access=free |issn=0035-8711|arxiv=2111.00558 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Luciano |first=Giuseppe Gaetano |date=2022-11-24 |title=Gravity and Cosmology in Kaniadakis Statistics: Current Status and Future Challenges |journal=Entropy |language=en |volume=24 |issue=12 |page=1712 |doi=10.3390/e24121712 |doi-access=free |issn=1099-4300 |pmc=9777509 |pmid=36554117|bibcode=2022Entrp..24.1712L }}</ref> [[astrophysics]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Carvalho |first1=J. == Mathematical formalism ==
The mathematical formalism of κ-statistics is generated by κ-deformed functions, especially the κ-exponential function.

=== κ-exponential function ===
[[File:Kappa exponential function plot.png|thumb|353x353px|Plot of the κ-exponential function <math>\exp_\kappa(x)</math> for three different κ-values. The solid black curve corresponding to the ordinary exponential function <math>\exp(x)</math> (<math>\kappa = 0 </math>).]]
The Kaniadakis exponential (or κ-exponential) function is a one-parameter generalization of an exponential function, given by:

<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (x) = \begin{cases}
\Big(\sqrt{1+\kappa^2 x^2}+\kappa x \Big)^\frac{1}{\kappa} & \text{if } 0 < \kappa < 1. \\[6pt]
\exp(x) & \text{if }\kappa = 0, \\[8pt]
\end{cases}</math>
with <math>\exp_{-\kappa} (x) = \exp_\kappa (x) </math>.

The κ-exponential for <math>0 < \kappa < 1 </math> can also be written in the form:

<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (x) = \exp\Bigg(\frac{1}{\kappa} \text{arsinh} (\kappa x)\Bigg).
</math>
The first five terms of the [[Taylor series|Taylor expansion]] of <math>\exp_\kappa(x)</math> are given by:
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (x) = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2} + (1 - \kappa^2) \frac{x^3}{3!} + (1 - 4 \kappa^2) \frac{x^4}{4!} + \cdots
</math>
where the first three are the same as a typical [[exponential function]].

'''Basic properties'''

The κ-exponential function has the following properties of an exponential function:
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (x) \in \mathbb{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R})</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dx}\exp_\kappa (x) > 0</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\exp_\kappa (x) > 0</math>
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (-\infty) = 0^+</math>
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (0) = 1</math>
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (+\infty) = +\infty</math>
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa (x) \exp_\kappa (-x) = -1</math>
For a [[real number]] <math>r</math>, the κ-exponential has the property:
<math display="block">\Big[\exp_\kappa (x)\Big]^r = \exp_{\kappa/r} (rx).</math>

=== κ-logarithm function ===
[[File:Kaniadakis kappa log function.png|thumb|347x347px|Plot of the κ-logarithmic function <math>\ln_\kappa(x)</math> for three different κ-values. The solid black curve corresponding to the ordinary logarithmic function <math>\ln(x)</math> (<math>\kappa = 0 </math>).]]
The Kaniadakis logarithm (or κ-logarithm) is a relativistic one-parameter generalization of the ordinary logarithm function,
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (x) = \begin{cases}
\frac{x^\kappa - x^{-\kappa}}{2\kappa} & \text{if } 0 < \kappa < 1, \\[8pt]
\ln(x) & \text{if }\kappa = 0, \\[8pt]
\end{cases}</math>
with <math>\ln_{-\kappa} (x) = \ln_\kappa (x)</math>, which is the [[inverse function]] of the κ-exponential:

<math display="block">\ln_\kappa\left( \exp_\kappa(x)\right) = \exp_\kappa\left( \ln_\kappa(x)\right) = x.</math>
The κ-logarithm for <math>0 < \kappa < 1</math> can also be written in the form:

<math>\ln_\kappa(x) = \frac{1}{\kappa}\sinh\Big(\kappa \ln(x)\Big)</math>

The first three terms of the [[Taylor series|Taylor expansion]] of <math>\ln_\kappa(x)</math> are given by:

<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (1+x) = x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \left( 1 + \frac{\kappa^2}{2}\right) \frac{x^3}{3} - \cdots</math>

following the rule

<math display="block"> \ln_\kappa(1+x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n(\kappa)\,(-1)^{n-1} \,\frac{x^n}{n} </math>

with <math> b_1(\kappa)= 1</math>, and

<math display="block"> b_{n}(\kappa) (x) = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } n = 1, \\[8pt]
\frac{1}{2}\Big(1-\kappa\Big)\Big(1-\frac{\kappa}{2}\Big)...
\Big(1-\frac{\kappa}{n-1}\Big) \,+\,\frac{1}{2}\Big(1+\kappa\Big)\Big(1+\frac{\kappa}{2}\Big) \dots
\Big(1+\frac{\kappa}{n-1}\Big) & \text{for } n > 1, \\[8pt]
\end{cases} </math>

where <math> b_n(0)=1 </math> and <math> b_n(-\kappa)=b_n(\kappa) </math>. The two first terms of the [[Taylor series|Taylor expansion]] of <math>\ln_\kappa(x)
</math> are the same as an [[Logarithm|ordinary logarithmic function]].

'''Basic properties'''

The κ-logarithm function has the following properties of a [[logarithm|logarithmic]] function:
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (x) \in \mathbb{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^+)</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dx}\ln_\kappa (x) > 0</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\ln_\kappa (x) < 0</math>
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (0^+) = -\infty</math>
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (1) = 0</math>
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (+\infty) = +\infty</math>
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (1/x) = -\ln_\kappa (x)</math>
For a real number <math>r</math>, the κ-logarithm has the property:
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa (x^r) = r \ln_{r \kappa} (x)</math>

=== κ-Algebra ===

==== κ-sum ====
For any <math>x,y \in \mathbb{R}</math> and <math>|\kappa| < 1</math>, the Kaniadakis sum (or κ-sum) is defined by the following composition law:
<math display="block">x\mathop\oplus^\kappa y = x\sqrt{1+\kappa^2y^2}+y\sqrt{1+\kappa^2x^2} , </math>
that can also be written in form:
<math display="block">x\mathop\oplus^\kappa y = {1\over\kappa}\,\sinh \left(\operatorname{arsinh}(\kappa x)\,+\,\operatorname{arsinh}(\kappa y)\right), </math>
where the ordinary sum is a particular case in the [[classical limit]] <math>\kappa \to 0 </math>: <math>x \mathop\oplus^0 y = x + y </math>.

The κ-sum, like the ordinary sum, has the following properties:
# associativity: <math display="block">(x\mathop\oplus^\kappa y)\mathop\oplus^\kappa z = x \mathop\oplus^\kappa (y \mathop\oplus^\kappa z)</math>
# neutral element: <math display="block">x \mathop\oplus^\kappa 0 = 0 \mathop\oplus^\kappa x = x </math>
# opposite element: <math display="block">x\mathop\oplus^\kappa(-x)=(-x) \mathop\oplus^\kappa x=0 </math>
# commutativity: <math display="block">x\mathop\oplus^\kappa y=y\mathop\oplus^\kappa x </math>
The κ-difference <math>\mathop\ominus^\kappa</math> is given by <math>x\mathop\ominus^\kappa y = x \mathop\oplus^\kappa(-y)</math>.

The fundamental property <math>\exp_\kappa(-x)\exp_\kappa(x)=1</math> arises as a special case of the more general expression below: <math>\exp_\kappa(x)\exp_\kappa(y)=exp_\kappa(x\mathop\oplus^\kappa y)</math>

Furthermore, the κ-functions and the κ-sum present the following relationships:
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa(x\,y) = \ln_\kappa(x) \mathop\oplus^\kappa\ln_\kappa(y)
</math>

==== κ-product ====
For any <math>x,y \in \mathbb{R}</math> and <math>|\kappa| < 1</math>, the Kaniadakis product (or κ-product) is defined by the following composition law:
<math display="block">x \mathop\otimes^\kappa y = {1\over\kappa} \,\sinh \left({1\over\kappa} \,\operatorname{arsinh}(\kappa x)\,\operatorname{arsinh}(\kappa y)\right),
</math>
where the ordinary product is a particular case in the classical limit <math>\kappa \to 0 </math>: <math>x \mathop\otimes^0 y = x \times y = xy </math>.

The κ-product, like the ordinary product, has the following properties:
# associativity: <math display="block">\left(x \mathop\otimes^\kappa y\right) \mathop\otimes^\kappa z = x \mathop\otimes^\kappa \left(y \mathop\otimes^\kappa z\right)</math>
# neutral element:<math display="block">x \mathop\otimes^\kappa I = I \mathop\otimes^\kappa x = x \quad \text{for} \quad I = \kappa^{-1}\sinh \kappa \mathop\oplus^\kappa x=x </math>
# inverse element: <math display="block">x \mathop\otimes^\kappa\overline x= \overline x \mathop\otimes^\kappa x=I  \quad \text{for} \quad \overline x = \kappa^{-1}\sinh\left(\kappa^2/\operatorname{arsinh}(\kappa x)\right) </math>
# commutativity: <math display="block">x\mathop\otimes^\kappa y=y\mathop\otimes^\kappa x </math>
The κ-division <math>\mathop\oslash^\kappa</math> is given by <math>x \mathop\oslash^\kappa y = x\mathop\otimes^\kappa\overline y</math>.

The κ-sum <math>\mathop\oplus^\kappa</math> and the κ-product <math>\mathop\otimes^\kappa</math> obey the distributive law: <math>z \mathop\otimes^\kappa \left(x \mathop\oplus^\kappa y\right) = \left(z \mathop\otimes^\kappa x\right) \mathop\oplus^\kappa \left(z \mathop\otimes^\kappa y\right) </math>.

The fundamental property <math>\ln_\kappa(1/x)=-\ln_\kappa(x)</math> arises as a special case of the more general expression below:

<math display="block">\ln_\kappa(x\,y) = \ln_\kappa(x) \mathop\oplus^\kappa \ln_\kappa(y)</math>

Furthermore, the κ-functions and the κ-product present the following relationships:
<math display="block">\exp_\kappa(x) \mathop\otimes^\kappa \exp_\kappa(y) = \exp_\kappa(x\,+\,y)</math>
<math display="block">\ln_\kappa(x\,\mathop\otimes^\kappa\,y) = \ln_\kappa(x) + \ln_\kappa(y)</math>

=== κ-Calculus ===

==== κ-Differential====
The Kaniadakis differential (or κ-differential) of <math>x</math> is defined by:
<math display="block">\mathrm{d}_\kappa x = \frac{\mathrm{d}\,x}{\displaystyle{\sqrt{1+\kappa^2\,x^2} }}.</math>

So, the κ-derivative of a function <math>f(x)</math> is related to the [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]] derivative through:
<math display="block"> \frac{\mathrm{d} f(x)}{\mathrm{d}_\kappa x} = \gamma_\kappa (x) \frac{\mathrm{d} f(x)}{\mathrm{d} x} , </math>
where <math> \gamma_\kappa(x) = \sqrt{1+\kappa^2 x^2}</math> is the [[Lorentz factor]]. The ordinary derivative <math>\frac{\mathrm{d} f(x)}{\mathrm{d} x} </math> is a particular case of κ-derivative <math>\frac{\mathrm{d} f(x)}{\mathrm{d}_\kappa x}</math> in the classical limit <math>\kappa \rightarrow 0</math>.

==== κ-Integral====
The Kaniadakis integral (or κ-integral) is the inverse operator of the κ-derivative defined through
<math display="block">\int \mathrm{d}_\kappa x \,\, f(x)= \int \frac{\mathrm{d}\, x}{\sqrt{1+\kappa^2\,x^2}}\,\,f(x) ,</math>
which recovers the ordinary integral in the classical limit <math>\kappa \to 0</math>.

=== κ-Trigonometry===

==== κ-Cyclic Trigonometry====
[[File:Kappa_trigonometric_sink_cosk.gif|alt=Plot of the κ-sine and κ-cosine functions for κ =0 (black curve) and κ&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.1 (blue curve).|thumb|643x643px|'''[click on the figure]''' Plot of the κ-sine and κ-cosine functions for <math>\kappa = 0</math> (black curve) and <math>\kappa = 0.1</math> (blue curve).]]
The Kaniadakis cyclic trigonometry (or κ-cyclic trigonometry) is based on the κ-cyclic sine (or κ-sine) and κ-cyclic cosine (or κ-cosine) functions defined by:
<math display="block">\sin_\kappa(x) =\frac{\exp_\kappa(ix) -\exp_\kappa(-ix)}{2i} ,</math>
<math display="block">\cos_\kappa(x) =\frac{\exp_\kappa(ix) +\exp_\kappa(-ix)}{2} ,</math>
where the κ-generalized [[Euler's formula|Euler formula]] is
<math display="block"> \exp_\kappa(\pm ix)=\cos_\kappa(x)\pm i\sin_\kappa(x) .</math>

The κ-cyclic trigonometry preserves fundamental expressions of the ordinary cyclic trigonometry, which is a special case in the limit ''κ'' → 0, such as:
<math display="block">\cos_\kappa^2(x) + \sin_\kappa^2(x) = 1 </math>
<math display="block">\sin_\kappa(x \mathop\oplus^\kappa y) = \sin_\kappa(x) \cos_\kappa(y) + \cos_\kappa(x) \sin_\kappa(y) .</math>

The κ-cyclic tangent and κ-cyclic cotangent functions are given by:
<math display="block"> \tan_\kappa(x)=\frac{\sin_\kappa(x)}{\cos_\kappa(x)} </math>
<math display="block"> \cot_\kappa(x)=\frac{\cos_\kappa(x)}{\sin_\kappa(x)} .</math>

The κ-cyclic trigonometric functions become the [[Trigonometric functions|ordinary trigonometric function]] in the classical limit <math>\kappa \to 0</math>.

'''κ-Inverse cyclic function'''

The Kaniadakis inverse cyclic functions (or κ-inverse cyclic functions) are associated to the κ-logarithm:
<math display="block"> \arcsin_\kappa(x) = -i\ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}+ix\right), </math>
<math display="block"> \arccos_\kappa(x) = -i\ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{x^2-1}+x\right) ,</math>
<math display="block"> \arctan_\kappa(x) = i \ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{\frac{1-ix}{1+ix}}\right) ,</math>
<math display="block"> \arccot_\kappa(x) = i \ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{\frac{ix+1}{ix-1}}\right) .</math>

==== κ-Hyperbolic Trigonometry====
The Kaniadakis hyperbolic trigonometry (or κ-hyperbolic trigonometry) is based on the κ-hyperbolic sine and κ-hyperbolic cosine given by:
<math display="block">\sinh_\kappa(x) =\frac{\exp_\kappa(x) -\exp_\kappa(-x)}{2} ,</math>
<math display="block">\cosh_\kappa(x) =\frac{\exp_\kappa(x) +\exp_\kappa(-x)}{2} ,</math>
where the κ-Euler formula is
<math display="block"> \exp_\kappa(\pm x)=\cosh_\kappa(x)\pm \sinh_\kappa(x) .</math>

The κ-hyperbolic tangent and κ-hyperbolic cotangent functions are given by:
<math display="block"> \tanh_\kappa(x)=\frac{\sinh_\kappa(x)}{\cosh_\kappa(x)} </math>
<math display="block"> \coth_\kappa(x)=\frac{\cosh_\kappa(x)}{\sinh_\kappa(x)}. </math>

The κ-hyperbolic trigonometric functions become the [[Hyperbolic functions|ordinary hyperbolic trigonometric functions]] in the classical limit <math>\kappa \to 0</math>.

From the κ-Euler formula and the property <math>\exp_\kappa(-x)\exp_\kappa(x)=1</math> the fundamental expression of κ-hyperbolic trigonometry is given as follows:
<math display="block">\cosh_\kappa^2(x)- \sinh_\kappa^2(x)=1</math>

'''κ-Inverse hyperbolic function'''

The Kaniadakis [[inverse hyperbolic functions]] (or κ-inverse hyperbolic functions) are associated to the κ-logarithm:
<math display="block"> \operatorname{arsinh}_\kappa(x)=\ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right), </math>
<math display="block"> \operatorname{arcosh}_\kappa(x)=\ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{x^2-1}+x\right), </math>
<math display="block"> \operatorname{artanh}_\kappa(x)=\ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+x}{1-x}}\right), </math>
<math display="block"> \operatorname{arcoth}_\kappa(x)=\ln_\kappa\left(\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}\right), </math>
in which are valid the following relations:
<math display="block"> \operatorname{arsinh}_\kappa(x) = \operatorname{sign}(x)\operatorname{arcosh}_\kappa\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}\right), </math>
<math display="block"> \operatorname{arsinh}_\kappa(x) = \operatorname{artanh}_\kappa\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\right) ,</math>
<math display="block"> \operatorname{arsinh}_\kappa(x) = \operatorname{arcoth}_\kappa\left(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{x}\right) .</math>
The κ-cyclic and κ-hyperbolic trigonometric functions are connected by the following relationships:
<math display="block"> {\sin}_\kappa(x) = -i\operatorname{sinh}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\cos}_\kappa(x) = \operatorname{cosh}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\tan}_\kappa(x) = -i\operatorname{tanh}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\cot}_\kappa(x) = i\operatorname{coth}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\arcsin}_\kappa(x)=-i\,\operatorname{arsinh}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\arccos}_\kappa(x)\neq -i\,\operatorname{arcosh}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\arctan}_\kappa(x)=-i\,\operatorname{artanh}_\kappa(ix), </math>
<math display="block"> {\arccot}_\kappa(x)=i\,\operatorname{arcoth}_\kappa(ix). </math>

=== Kaniadakis entropy ===
The Kaniadakis statistics is based on the Kaniadakis κ-entropy, which is defined through:
<math display="block">S_\kappa{\left(p\right)} = -\sum_i p_i \ln_\kappa\left(p_i\right) = \sum_i p_i \ln_\kappa \left(\frac{1}{p_i} \right)</math>
where <math display="inline">p = \left\{p_i = p(x_i); x \in \mathbb{R}; i = 1, 2, \dots, N; \sum_i p_i = 1\right\}</math> is a [[probability distribution]] function defined for a [[random variable]] <math>X</math>, and <math>0 \leq |\kappa| < 1</math> is the entropic index.

The Kaniadakis κ-entropy is thermodynamically and Lesche stable<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abe |first1=S. |last2=Kaniadakis |first2=G. |last3=Scarfone |first3=A. M. |year=2004 |orig-date=2004 |title=Stabilities of generalized entropies |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General |publication-date=2004 |volume=37 |issue=44 |pages=10513–10519|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/37/44/004 |arxiv=cond-mat/0401290 |bibcode=2004JPhA...3710513A |s2cid=16080176 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=G. |date=2001 |title=H-theorem and generalized entropies within the framework of nonlinear kinetics |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0375960101005436 |journal=Physics Letters A |language=en |volume=288 |issue=5–6 |pages=283–291 |doi=10.1016/S0375-9601(01)00543-6|arxiv=cond-mat/0109192 |bibcode=2001PhLA..288..283K |s2cid=119445915 }}</ref> and obeys the Shannon-Khinchin axioms of continuity, maximality, generalized additivity and expandability.

== Kaniadakis distributions ==
{{main|Kaniadakis distribution}}

A '''[[Kaniadakis distribution]]''' (or '''''κ''-distribution''') is a [[probability distribution]] derived from the maximization of Kaniadakis entropy under appropriate constraints. In this regard, several probability distributions emerge for analyzing a wide variety of phenomenology associated with experimental power-law tailed statistical distributions.

{{main|Kaniadakis Exponential distribution}}

{{main|Kaniadakis Gaussian distribution}}

== Kaniadakis integral transform ==

=== κ-Laplace Transform ===
The Kaniadakis Laplace transform (or κ-Laplace transform) is a κ-deformed [[integral transform]] of the [[Laplace transform|ordinary Laplace transform]]. The κ-Laplace transform converts a function <math>f</math> of a real variable <math>t</math> to a new function <math>F_\kappa(s)</math> in the complex frequency domain, represented by the complex variable <math>s</math>. This κ-integral transform is defined as:<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Kaniadakis |first=Giorgio |date=2013-09-25 |title=Theoretical Foundations and Mathematical Formalism of the Power-Law Tailed Statistical Distributions |journal=Entropy |language=en |volume=15 |issue=12 |pages=3983–4010 |doi=10.3390/e15103983 |arxiv=1309.6536 |bibcode=2013Entrp..15.3983K |issn=1099-4300|doi-access=free }}</ref>
<math display="block">F_\kappa(s) = \mathcal{L}_\kappa\{f(t)\}(s)=\int_0^\infty \!f(t) \,[\exp_\kappa(-t)]^s\,dt </math>
The inverse κ-Laplace transform is given by:
<math display="block">
f(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}_\kappa\{F_\kappa(s)\}(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i \infty}^{c+i \infty}\!F_\kappa(s) \,\frac{[\exp_\kappa(t)]^s}{\sqrt{1+\kappa^2t^2}}\,ds
</math>
The [[Laplace transform|ordinary Laplace transform]] and its [[Inverse Laplace transform|inverse transform]] are recovered as <math>\kappa \to 0</math>.

'''Properties'''

Let two functions <math>f(t) = {\cal L}^{-1}_\kappa\{F_\kappa(s)\}(t)</math> and <math>g(t) = {\cal L}^{-1}_\kappa\{G_\kappa(s)\}(t)</math>, and their respective κ-Laplace transforms <math>F_\kappa(s)</math> and <math>G_\kappa(s)</math>, the following table presents the main properties of κ-Laplace transform:<ref name=":1" />
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Properties of the κ-Laplace transform
|-
!Property
! scope="col" | <math> f(t) </math>
! scope="col" | <math> F_\kappa(s) </math>
|-
|[[Linearity]]
| <math> a\, f (t)+ b\, g (t) </math>
| <math> a\, F_\kappa (s)+ b\, G_\kappa (s) </math>
|-
|Time scaling
| <math> f(at) </math>
| <math> \frac{1}{a}\, F_{\kappa / a} (\frac{s}{a}) </math>
|-
|Frequency shifting
| <math> f(t)\, [\exp_\kappa(-t)]^{a} </math>
| <math> F_\kappa(s-a) </math>
|-
|[[Derivative]]
| <math> \frac{d\, f(t)}{dt} </math>
| <math> s\, {\cal L}_\kappa\left \{\frac{f(t)}{\sqrt{1+\kappa^2 t^2}}\right \}(s)-f(0) </math>
|-
|[[Derivative]]
| <math> \frac{d}{dt} \, \sqrt{1+\kappa^2 t^2} \, f(t) </math>
| <math> s \, F_\kappa (s) -f(0) </math>
|-
| Time-domain [[Integral|integration]]
| <math> \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\kappa^2 t^2}}\, \int_0^t f(w)dw </math>
| <math> \frac{1}{s} \, F_\kappa (s) </math>
|-
|
| <math> f(t)\, [\ln (\exp_\kappa(t))]^n </math>
| <math> (-1)^n \frac{d^{n} F_\kappa(s)}{ds^n} </math>
|-
|
| <math> f(t) \,[\ln (\exp_\kappa(t))]^{-n} </math>
| <math> \int_s^{+\infty}dw_{n} \int_{w_n}^{+\infty}dw_{n-1}...\int_{w_3}^{+\infty}dw_{2}\int_{w_2}^{+\infty}dw_{1} \,F_\kappa(w_1) </math>
|-
|Dirac delta-function
| <math> \delta (t-\tau) </math>
| <math> [\exp_\kappa(-\tau)]^s </math>
|-
|Heaviside unit function
| <math> u(t-\tau) </math>
| <math> \frac{s\sqrt{1+\kappa^2 \tau^2}+\kappa^2 \tau}{s^2-\kappa^2}\, [\exp_\kappa(-\tau)]^{s} </math>
|-
|Power function
| <math> t^{\nu-1} </math>
| <math> \frac{s^2}{s^2-\kappa^2\nu^2}\,\frac{\Gamma_{\frac{\kappa}{s}}(\nu+1)}{\nu\, s^{\nu}}=\frac{s}{s+|\kappa|\nu}\, \frac{\Gamma (\nu)}{|2\kappa|^{\nu}}\, \frac{\Gamma\left( \frac{s}{|2\kappa|} - \frac{\nu}{2} \right )} {\Gamma\left( \frac{s}{|2\kappa|} + \frac{\nu}{2} \right )} </math>
|-
|Power function
| <math> t^{2m-1}, \ \ m \in Z^+ </math>
| <math> \frac{(2m-1)!}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left[s^2-(2j)^2\kappa^2\right] } </math>
|-
|Power function
| <math> t^{2m}, \ \ m \in Z^+ </math>
| <math> \frac{(2m)!\, s}{\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}\left[s^2-(2j-1)^2\kappa^2\right] } </math>
|}

The κ-Laplace transforms presented in the latter table reduce to the corresponding [[Laplace transform|ordinary Laplace transforms]] in the classical limit <math>\kappa \to 0</math>.

=== κ-Fourier Transform ===
The Kaniadakis Fourier transform (or κ-Fourier transform) is a κ-deformed integral transform of the ordinary [[Fourier transform]], which is consistent with the κ-algebra and the κ-calculus. The κ-Fourier transform is defined as:<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Scarfone |first=A.M. |date=2017 |title=κ -deformed Fourier transform |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0378437117302881 |journal=Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and Its Applications |language=en |volume=480 |pages=63–78 |doi=10.1016/j.physa.2017.03.036|arxiv=2206.06869 |bibcode=2017PhyA..480...63S |s2cid=126079408 }}</ref>

<math display="block">
{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega) = {1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}f(x)\,
\exp_\kappa(-x\otimes_\kappa\omega)^i\,d_\kappa x
</math>

which can be rewritten as

<math display="block">
{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega)={1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}}\int\limits_{-\infty}\limits^{+\infty}f(x)\,
{\exp(-i\,x_{\{\kappa\}}\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}})\over\sqrt{1+\kappa^2\,x^2}} \,d x
</math>

where <math>x_{\{\kappa\}}=\frac{1}{\kappa}\, \operatorname{arsinh}
\,(\kappa\,x)</math> and <math>\omega_{\{\kappa\}}=\frac{1}{\kappa}\, \operatorname{arsinh}
\,(\kappa\,\omega)</math>. The κ-Fourier transform imposes an asymptotically log-periodic behavior by deforming the parameters <math>x</math> and <math>\omega</math> in addition to a damping factor, namely <math>\sqrt{1+\kappa^2\,x^2}</math>.

[[File:Kaniadakis fourier nucleo cdf.png|thumb|502x502px|Real (top panel) and imaginary (bottom panel) part of the kernel <math>h_\kappa(x,\omega)</math> for typical <math>\kappa</math>-values and <math>\omega = 1</math>.]]

The kernel of the κ-Fourier transform is given by:

<math display="block"> h_\kappa(x,\omega) = \frac{\exp\left( i \, x_{\{\kappa\}}\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}}\right)}\sqrt{1+\kappa^2\,x^2} </math>

The inverse κ-Fourier transform is defined as:<ref name=":2" />

<math display="block"> \mathcal{F}_\kappa[\hat{f}\!(\omega)](x) = {1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}\!(\omega) \exp_\kappa(\omega \otimes_\kappa x)^i\,d_\kappa \omega </math>

Let <math>u_\kappa(x) = \frac 1 \kappa \cosh\Big(\kappa\ln(x) \Big)</math>, the following table shows the κ-Fourier transforms of several notable functions:<ref name=":2" />
{| class="wikitable"
|+ κ-Fourier transform of several functions
|-
!
! scope="col" | <math>f(x)</math>
! scope="col" | <math> {\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega) </math>
|-
| Step function
| <math> \theta(x) </math>
| <math> \sqrt{2\,\pi}\,\delta(\omega)+{1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}\,i\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}}}</math>
|-
| Modulation
| <math> \cos_\kappa(a \mathop\oplus^\kappa x) </math>
| <math> \sqrt{\pi\over2}\,u_\kappa(\exp_\kappa(a))\,\left(\delta(\omega+a)+\delta(\omega-a)\right) </math>
|-
| Causal <math>\kappa</math>-exponential
| <math> \theta(x)\,\exp_\kappa(-a \mathop\otimes^\kappa x) </math>
| <math> {1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}}{1\over a_{\{\kappa\}}+i\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}}} </math>
|-
| Symmetric <math>\kappa</math>-exponential
| <math> \exp_\kappa(-a \mathop\otimes^\kappa |x|) </math>
| <math> \sqrt{2\over\pi}\,{a_{\{\kappa\}}\over a_{\{\kappa\}}^2+\omega_{\{\kappa\}}^2} </math>
|-
| Constant
| <math> 1 </math>
| <math> \sqrt{2\,\pi}\,\delta(\omega) </math>
|-
| <math>\kappa</math>-Phasor
| <math>\exp_\kappa\,(a \mathop\otimes^\kappa x)^i </math>
| <math> \sqrt{2\,\pi}\,u_\kappa(\exp_\kappa(a))\,\delta(\omega-a)</math>
|-
| Impuslse
| <math> \delta(x-a) </math>
| <math> {1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}}{\exp_\kappa\,(\omega \mathop\otimes^\kappa a)^i\over u_\kappa\left(\exp_\kappa\,(a)\right)} </math>
|-
| Signum
| Sgn<math>(x)</math>
| <math>\sqrt{2\over\pi}\,\,{1\over i\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}}}</math>
|-
| Rectangular
| <math> \Pi\left({x\over a}\right) </math>
| <math> \sqrt{2\over\pi}\,\,a_{\{\kappa\}}\,\operatorname{sinc}_\kappa(\omega \mathop\otimes^\kappa a) </math>
|}

The κ-deformed version of the Fourier transform preserves the main properties of the ordinary Fourier transform, as summarized in the following table.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ κ-Fourier properties
|-
! scope="col" | <math>f(x)</math>
! scope="col" | <math> {\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega) </math>
|-
| Linearity
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa[\alpha\,f(x)+\beta\,g(x)](\omega)=\alpha\,{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega)+\beta\,{\cal F}_\kappa[g(x)](\omega) </math>
|-
| Scaling
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[f(\alpha\,x)\right](\omega)={1\over\alpha}\,{\cal F}_{\kappa^\prime}\left[f(x)\right](\omega^\prime) </math> <br /> where <math> \kappa^\prime=\kappa/\alpha</math> and <math>\omega^\prime=(a/\kappa)\,\sinh\left(\operatorname{arsinh}(\kappa\,\omega)/a^2\right) </math>
|-
| <math>\kappa</math>-Scaling
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[f(\alpha \mathop\otimes^\kappa x)\right](\omega)={1\over\alpha_{\{\kappa\}}}\,{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)]\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathop\otimes^\kappa\omega\right) </math>
|-
| Complex conjugation
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\big[f(x)\big]^{\ast}(\omega)={\cal F}_\kappa\big[f(x)\big](-\omega) </math>
|-
| Duality
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\Big[{\cal F}_\kappa\big[f(x)\big](\nu)\Big](\omega)=f(-\omega) </math>
|-
| Reverse
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[f(-x)\right](\omega)={\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](-\omega) </math>
|-
| <math> \kappa</math>-Frequency shift
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[\exp_\kappa (\omega_0 \mathop\otimes^\kappa x)^if(x)\right](\omega)={\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega\mathop\ominus^\kappa\omega_0) </math>
|-
| <math>\kappa</math>-Time shift
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[f(x \,\mathop\oplus^\kappa\,x_0)\right](\omega)=\exp_\kappa (\omega\,\mathop\otimes^\kappa\, x_0)^i\, {\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega) </math>
|-
| Transform of <math>\kappa</math>-derivative
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[\frac{d\,f(x)}{d_\kappa x}\right](\omega)=i\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}}\,{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega) </math>
|-
| <math>\kappa</math>-Derivative of transform
| <math> \frac{d}{d_\kappa\omega}\,{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega)=-i\,\omega_{\{\kappa\}}\,{\cal F}_\kappa\left[x_{\{\kappa\}}\,f(x)\right](\omega) </math>
|-
| Transform of integral
| <math>{\cal F}_\kappa\left[\int_{-\infty}^x f(y)\,dy\right](\omega) = {1\over i \omega_{\{\kappa\}}}{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega) + 2\pi \, {\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](0)\,\delta(\omega) </math>
|-
| <math>\kappa</math>-Convolution
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[(f \,\mathop\circledast^\kappa\, g)(x)\right](\omega)=\sqrt{2\,\pi}\,{\cal F}_\kappa[f(x)](\omega)\,{\cal F}_\kappa[g(x)](\omega) </math> <br /> where <math> (f \,\mathop\circledast^\kappa\, g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y) \, g(x \mathop\ominus^\kappa y) \,d_\kappa y </math>
|-
| Modulation
| <math> {\cal F}_\kappa\left[f(x)\,g(x)\right](\omega)={1\over\sqrt{2\,\pi}}\left({\cal F}_\kappa\left[f(x)\right] \,\mathop\circledast^\kappa\, {\cal F}_\kappa\left[g(x)\right]\right)(\omega) </math>
|}

The properties of the κ-Fourier transform presented in the latter table reduce to the corresponding [[Fourier transform|ordinary Fourier transforms]] in the classical limit <math>\kappa \to 0</math>.
